title: The timeline zooms, so a recording longer than a few seconds can be cut
goal: The timeline draws the whole document across whatever width the window happens to be. An eight second recording fits and reads fine. A five minute one, which is what a real screen recording is, becomes a bar a few hundred pixels wide where every cut is a guess and the waveform under it is a smear. Give the timeline a zoom, so you can open out the second you are working on and still see where you are in the whole thing.
notes:
From the 2026-09-20-a-recording-is-a-document audit rough list, word for word: "The timeline's local bar has no zoom. An eight second recording fits the width; a five minute one would be unreadable. D8 puts timeline zoom in the timeline's own bar and it is not built."

VERIFIED still missing on 2026-09-21: Sources/Photonz/CutStrip.swift is 148 lines and contains no zoom, no scale and no pixels-per-second; the strip is laid out against the document duration and the available width.

The design already says where it goes. docs/design/video-surface.md:111: "Timeline zoom, blade, and what is scoped to the timeline | .tlbar, the timeline's own local bar | D8's last row. Today only video.html draws a zoom at all."

Why it is worth doing before more video features rather than after: the 2026-09-21-video-audio audit already has to ask "Is the waveform legible enough to aim a cut at a word, at the width your timeline actually is?" Every feature added to the timeline from here (captions, transitions, components with a start and an end) makes the unzoomed strip more crowded, so each one lands on a surface that is already too small to read.
acceptance: The timeline can be zoomed in and out, and a five minute recording can be opened out far enough to put a cut on a particular word
Zooming keeps the playhead where you are looking rather than jumping you to the start
When the timeline is zoomed in you can still tell where you are in the whole document and get back out in one gesture
Waveforms and piece joins redraw at the zoomed scale rather than being stretched, so the detail you zoomed in for is actually there
The zoom control lives in the timeline's own local bar, which is where D8 and docs/design/video-surface.md put it, not in the transport
Scrubbing and cutting stay smooth at every zoom level on a five minute recording
audit written under queue/audits/, and anything left rough is filed as a follow-up task if it clears the follow-up bar and written into this task log if it does not

log.note: core landed: TimelineZoom + TimelineSpan in PhotonzCore, MotionStripRuler windowed (startMS, fraction(spanningMS:), msSpanning). 26 new tests written first, whole suite green (8952 tests).

adversarial review before building, written into the task as the contract asks. (1) The mock (video.html) draws a zoom SLIDER. Rejected: five minutes opens out 300x, so nine tenths of a slider's travel is the first two seconds of useful range. Built a minus, a plus, a readout saying what is on screen, and Fit. (2) A first-time user has to be able to SEE there is a zoom, so it is a permanent control in the timeline's own bar rather than only a pinch. (3) Nothing decorative: no percentage readout (1200% says nothing about time), no blade (cutting is the playhead and B). (4) Shortest version that still delivers: window the ruler, four controls, an overview bar, and bounded drawing. The overview earns its place because a zoom CREATES the question 'where am I in the whole thing' and it also does the panning.

left rough, below the follow-up bar and recorded here rather than filed: (1) no keyboard shortcut for the zoom, left alone deliberately so plus and minus do not mean two different zooms in one window; (2) panning is the overview bar and a pinch only, because the lanes already scroll vertically and SwiftUI gives a view no sideways scroll without dropping to AppKit; (3) the window readout rounds to whole seconds so it can read 4:56 to 4:58 while the ruler counts tenths; (4) how far you opened out is forgotten when the document closes, which is deliberate for now (opening a recording restores the playhead, not the zoom); (5) a picked piece is drawn in solid accent, which makes its waveform hard to read at exactly the zoom where the waveform became worth reading -- worth watching, and if it shows up again it has earned a task. FILED instead: the-transport-says-the-arrow-keys-step-a-frame-a, because the transport's own tooltip promises a shortcut that edits your document instead.

The timeline opens out. Shipped in 249c3509 behind next-open-out-the-timeline, on by default in Next. The ruler (MotionStripRuler) now carries a window, so everything on the strip zooms through the one piece of arithmetic it was always laid out by; the control is in the timeline's own local bar (minus, plus, what is on screen said as two moments, Fit), a thin overview bar over the ruler says where you are in the whole recording and pans it, a pinch opens out around the point under the fingers, and playing pages the window along. Every zoom keeps the playhead where it is on screen. Verified: 26 core tests written before the code plus the whole suite green at 8952; a new walk open-out-the-timeline-walk that drives the real buttons on a document made five minutes long and leaves 7 real pictures of the window; and the timeline (7), trim (12), cut (9), motion (9) and clip (2) walk sets all passing. Audit: queue/audits/2026-09-22-timeline-zoom.json. Design: docs/design/video-surface.md section 13.
